utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution, together with Mr. Carmela Javier, and my name is Dan Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Eadaoin O'Brien, Tina Drolec, all of whom are assisting myself, my name is Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. I know you know it, Mr. Treanor, but it's a ritual: You are once again reminded that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, whole truth, and nothing else about the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was there anything from yesterday's proceedings that you wish to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one perhaps minor matter connected with the matter discussed in the closed session yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session. 15 [Closed session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what was the issue you wish to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a question about the capacity in which Zoran Lilic signed the documents we were looking at, and I believe I stated that he signed as President of the FRY. In fact, he signed as President of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we be bring Exhibit P215 onto the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit P215.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And could we go to page 18 in the English translation, and I don't know what page it will be in the B/C/S. It is right at the end of the document before all the attachments. So if we go to page 18 of the English translation. Sorry, yes, if we go back one, back to page 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, this was the exhibit we were looking at yesterday but we -- the pages that you were taken to were only up until page 12. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then if we can go over to page 18 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You just stated a moment ago that Zoran Lilic signed it in his capacity as President of the Supreme Defence Council as opposed to President of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if that is what -- is that what you can see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is reflected in the translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would ask perhaps that -- if we could have pages 1 to 18 of this document admitted into evidence. We, yesterday, only admitted pages 1 to 12. But given that this is to the end of the document before all of the annexes which can be seen on the previous page as -- that are attached and that is what makes up the additional 60-odd pages of this document, which I don't seek to tender at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And why can't we tender the first 12 pages and this last page only and leave the ones in between?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can do that, Your Honour. I was simply trying to keep the document in some sort of context before -- without all of its attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, then. Do we need to give this now a new -- it doesn't have to get a new number. Okay, fine. Then pages 1 to 18 will form Exhibit P215. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And obviously those pages would also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment this is a draft translation, and it would be the Prosecution's intention to seek a final translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was that issue not dealt with yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There will then -- do you want us to MFI this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can you mark it for identification, please, this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this will be Exhibit P215, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was there anything else in relation to the closed session testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May we move into open session, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, before we pick up from where we left off yesterday, I wish to revisit a number of documents from Thursday's hearing last week which we were unable to discuss because there was no English translation attached in e-court. First, at transcript page 1125, I took you to Rule 65 ter number 00441.01, which was the constitution of the FRY, 27th of April, 1992, and at transcript page 1126, I directed you to Article 135 of the constitution and I asked you who commanded the army of the FRY. However, as I've just said, that Rule 65 ter exhibit number did not have an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do have an English translation attached to a different Rule 65 ter number, but it's the same document. It's the constitution of the FRY. And that is Exhibit number -- Rule 65 ter number 7621, and I would ask that that be put on the screen. If we could go to page 06721. Could we go to page 44 of the English and page 46 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, do the provisions of Article 135 provide for who commands the army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the article states: "In war-time and peace-time the Army of Yugoslavia shall be under the command of the Presidents of the Republic, pursuant to decisions by the Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can also see, while it's on the screen, Article 134, that a law will be adopted which regulates the Army of Yugoslavia. And at transcript pages 1152 and 1153, you discussed Exhibit P197, the law on the army, which you said was legislated at the end of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the constitution, I don't know, since it's a 50 -- 50-page document, I would seek to tender this page which has the relevant article on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's page 44?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Page 44 of the English and page 46 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That page is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P229, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, also on Thursday you gave evidence about the SDS in BiH forming its own assembly in October of 1991. At transcript page 1164 I asked you what the SDS position was at that time with respect to remaining in a joint Yugoslavia, and you stated that they maintained their position pushing to remain in Yugoslavia and that the Assembly passed a resolution to that effect. I called for a Rule 65 ter exhibit which was then marked -- which was then admitted as P180, marked for identification, because no translation was attached in e-court. This has now been rectified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I would ask that Exhibit P180, MFI, is placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is this the decision, the English translation, is this the decision that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is on that page, but that's not the one that's been blown up. It's item number 2 on the page. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page of the English translation, please, and further down to the second decision. Can we go to the next page. I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is still an incomplete translation. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, also on Thursday, at transcript page 1070 you stated that on the 21st of December, 1991, the SDS in BiH declared their intention to proceed to the formation of their own republic by issuing a decision to that effect. I called for a Rule 65 ter exhibit which was then marked as Exhibit P181 and marked for identification because we didn't have an English translation. This has now been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I would call for P181, MFI, to be put on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is this the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I'm referring to is item number 21 on the Serbian page, in the lower right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go to page 2 of the English translation. Your Honour, I've been advised that it's the document with ERN 0044-8163, which is attached to that e-court 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is that the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is that the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now we see the English translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted, Exhibit P181, which is currently marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if it is already Exhibit P181, MFI, isn't it already admitted? Is this in addition to P181?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, this was the actual document that I was trying to take Mr. Treanor to but the translation hadn't been -- wasn't in e-court. So we've subsequently uploaded it and that's the document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you still want it to stay as an MFI?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I wish for it to be admitted, but it's currently P181, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted as Exhibit P181.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go back to P180. I've been advised that it is there but we're unable to link the document. If the registrar can go to the document which is 0040-0938, which is part of the 65 ter number 06655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The long and short of all those numbers is that we are going to P180, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, is this the document that you referred to on Thursday when -- that we had discussed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the English translation. In the Serbian it begins at the lower right of the page, item number 2, and it continues on the next page, as did the previous document we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that now, P180, MFI, be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that, in fact, this number -- this document is coming under a different 65 ter number from the one that P180, MFI, came, so would you prefer perhaps that we admit it under this 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and discard the previous number?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is the 65 ter number now here?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 06655, Your Honour, but the Exhibit P180 and all the details for it will now be given to this new document that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then shall we -- that exhibit, 06655, shall it be admitted into evidence and given an exhibit number as P180.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have also received an official translation for P178, MFI, which was referred to in the transcript at page 1059. If that could be brought up onto the screen, please. Your Honour, that was part of Rule 65 ter number 06688, and it is the document attached to e-court as 0214-4020-ET2. The document -- the English translation that's on the screen at the moment is the old translation. It has to be the document marked 0214-4020-ET2, which is attached to that Rule 65 ter number. The translation that's on the screen in the moment is in relation to MFI 152. The Rule 65 ter number is 06688. And I'm -- I do apologise. I was given the wrong ERN number. It is the ERN number SA04-1167-ET2. My apologies to the registrar. Your Honour, this is the official CLSS translation of Exhibit P178, and I would ask that that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit -- this translation is admitted into evidence and Exhibit P178, marked for identification, is now admitted as Exhibit 178.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for clarification, would counsel want the official CLSS translation to replace the draft translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we also have a CLSS translation for MFI -- P152, MFI, which is part of Exhibit -- Rule 65 ter number 06628, and it's the document that I spoke of a moment ago, 0214-4020-ET2. Your Honour, this is the exhibit that the Defence had an objection to, to the word "dictated by" as opposed to "decided upon," you may recall. This was discussed at transcript page 982 of the transcript. If we can turn to the second page, please -- sorry, no, it's on the first page. It's the first full paragraph that you can see on the screen, Your Honour, starting with "We must ensure unity in Serbia ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And now that "dictate" is supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The difference in the translation is the second sentence in that paragraph, starting "and as you know, borders are always dictated by the strong common, never by the weak ..." That, in the original translation said, "as you know, borders are always decided upon by the strong, never the weak ..." and there was the issue of -- because in Mr. Treanor's report, at paragraph, I think, 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On page 11. The Defence has been provided with a copy of this translation, and I presume that they don't maintain their objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is now official?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the CLSS translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this Exhibit P152, marked for identification, is admitted into evidence as Exhibit P152.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's two other exhibits marked for identification which are still outstanding and that's P151, MFI, and P161, MFI, and we are still waiting on those documents to come back from translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sutherland. May I suggest that when you do find the translations, just do the necessary and advise the registrar that we'll just mention it in court, rather than take all this time trying to change them from "marked for identification" to an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, we finished yesterday afternoon with you telling the Trial Chamber very briefly what had happened between December 1994 and August 1995. So in August 1995 did the -- did the FRY leadership discuss with the Bosnian Serb leadership the settling of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have Rule 65 ter number 06606.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the events that led to this discussion.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, at the beginning of August, after the beginning of the Croatian operation against the RSK, Slobodan Milosevic publicly appealed to Ratko Mladic and Alija Izetbegovic for peace, and the United States government started an initiative for peace with shuttle diplomacy being conducted by Richard Holbrooke who visited the capitals in the region and spoke to Mr. Milosevic, among others. At this point at the time of this meeting, the FRY leaders were meeting with the RSK leaders in order to develop a joint position in regard to forthcoming peace negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did both leaderships get together to discuss this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two meetings in August. The first meeting was on the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held in Dobanovci, outside of Belgrade, which was an Army of Yugoslavia facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was in attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a large number of the top leaders of the FRY and the RSK were present, including Zoran Lilic, Slobodan Milosevic, Momir Bulatovic, Radoje Kontic, Pavle Bulatovic, on the FRY side. And on the RS side, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Nikola Koljevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic, Zdravko Tolimir, Djordje Djukic, and Milan Gvero, all of whom were generals in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get clarity? I'm sorry, ma'am. Let me just hold this so that -- at page 13, lines 3 to 5, Mr. Treanor, you're saying at this point at the time of this meeting, the FRY leaders were meeting with the RSK leaders in order to develop a joint position in regard to forthcoming peace negotiations, and now I realise you're mentioning RS leaders as being present, not RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm sorry. I misspoke, Your Honour. It is RS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it should be "RS" at page 13?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, was anyone in attendance from the army, from the FRY?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the FRY side, from the army, Momcilo Perisic was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could go to pages -- page 2 of the English translation and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what did -- what did Slobodan Milosevic have to say at this session? Sorry, and the document that we have in front of us are the minutes of the 42nd -- sorry, the notes of the meeting held in Dobanovci on the 25th of August, 1995. What did Mr. Milosevic say at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had quite a bit to say, and he made several references to the -- what he saw as the goals that the Serbs should be pursuing in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did he see as the goals that they should be pursuing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he thought the most important thing was to obtain peace and recognition for the existence of RS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was Dr. Radovan Karadzic's response?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic pointed out to Mr. Milosevic some areas that he thought were important, geographical areas that he thought were important, that should be objects of the negotiations and that should be -- the possession of which for RS should be achieved in the course of his negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is this discussed on page 7 of the English translation and page 8 of the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 7 in the English contains part of that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just above the middle of the page. If I could just read those two -- three short paragraphs. "When President Karadzic heard about this inability to assist Republika Srpska, he asked President Milosevic: 'President, does this mean, then, that I shouldn't go to the Neretva and into Eastern Slavonia?'" The President of Serbia replied that what Karadzic was suggesting was a war option. "Does that mean we're giving up Republic of Serbian Krajina territory and a wider access to the sea?" Karadzic asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, what's the significance of this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here Dr. Karadzic is mentioning one of the accesses to the sea, which was one of the strategic goals that the RS leadership had adopted, and he seems to be concerned that Mr. Milosevic would not be pushing for this in negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, can pages 1 and 7 of the English translation be admitted into evidence, and page 1, 7, and 8 of the English -- B/C/S -- sorry, 8 and 9 of the B/C/S be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those pages will be Exhibit P230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, did this -- you said that there were two meetings between the FRY leadership and the Bosnian Serb leadership. You mentioned one on the 25th of August. When was the next meeting with the -- between the two leaderships?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next meeting took place on the 29th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Between those two meetings, did the Bosnian Serbs hold an Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 02160.01.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At this Assembly session, did Dr. Karadzic discuss what he hopes the Republika Srpska would achieve from the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 68 of the English translation and page 86 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did Dr. Karadzic say in this regard?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, among other things, I would direct the Court's attention to the bottom of the first paragraph in the English translation, the line beginning with "... channels and something." The first full sentence in that line reads: "We've drawn some maps into which a part of the Neretva Valley could be integrated, and, of course, access to the sea. The Drina should be clean. These are all priorities. The corridor must be wide." And at the bottom of the page, he makes some further comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What are those comments in relation to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the territories that he would like to see recognised as part of RS as a result of the negotiations. The fifth line from the bottom, toward the end: "I ask you another thing. So far we have been up to the task, we were a nation. Trebinje must equally care about Drvar and Drvar about Trebinje, otherwise, we are ruined. We absolutely cannot let ourselves get any ideas about them taking our traditional territories from us. To tell the truth, there are towns that we've grabbed for ourselves, and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how about in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica and Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance, they had to become ours and nobody is practically questioning it anymore. Between Grmec and Kozara, I think Milosevic must also know that, foreign negotiators have also been told this, between Grmec and Kozara, nothing can belong to anyone but us, because genocide was committed there, Serbian people have been killed there, and the number of Muslims grew 50 per cent because of the genocide and not because of some neutral development. Genocide was also committed in the Neretva Valley. There, that's all I wanted to say."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can pages 1 and 68 and 69 of the English translation and page 1 and 86 and 87 of the B/C/S be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P231, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have Rule 65 ter number 06653 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you mentioned a moment ago that this second meeting between the FRY and the RS leadership was held at the end of August 1995. What was -- what was the outcome of this meeting? If I could direct you to pages 18 and 19 of the English translation and page 16 of the B/C/S. Could you tell the Court the results of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The outcome of this meeting was a decision, indeed an agreement, witnessed by the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church, Pavle, who was there, that a joint delegation would be formed for peace delegations composed of representatives from the FRY and the RS, and that Slobodan Milosevic would have a -- the deciding vote in case there was any -- in case there was a disagreement within the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, was anyone present from the Army of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Momcilo Perisic was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And from the VRS army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic was present on this occasion as well as -- as well as the other generals who were at the other meeting, Zdravko Tolimir, Milan Gvero, and Djordje Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So basically what did Slobodan Milosevic -- what was his position at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the goals, the objectives, of the negotiations were concerned, we can see at the bottom of page 18 in the translation, in the final paragraph there: "Leadership of Republika Srpska requested from President Milosevic to set forth priorities that he would represent at the Conference with representatives of the Contact Group concerning the former BiH, which was done. President Milosevic wrote on a separate piece of paper that they were: "1) north corridor as broad as possible (especially in Brcko); 2) compactness of territory; 3) as many towns as possible; and 4) an access to the sea." At this point President Karadzic had something to say, and according to the record: "At President Karadzic's insistence, a list of priorities was amended with three more items: 5) area between Grmec and Kozara; 6) the Neretva basin; and 7) Serb Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, may pages 1, 18, and 19 of the English and page 1 and page 16 of the B/C/S be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P232, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what position did the Bosnian Serb leadership adopt on the eve of the Dayton negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Serb Assembly adopted its own resolution on territorial priorities at a session on the 22nd and 23rd of October, 1995, which was just a week or so before the beginning -- the scheduled beginning of the negotiations in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have Rule 65 ter number 02162 on the screen, please. If we could go to page 3 of the English translation and page 3 and then 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, does this document set out - on page 3 of the English translation and page 3 and over onto page 4 of the B/C/S - what the territorial priorities were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it sets out the territorial priorities as defined by the Bosnian Serb Assembly at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may pages 1 and 3 of the English translation and pages 1, 3, and 4 of the B/C/S be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P233, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we've lost the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just looking at the territorial priorities on page 3 of the English translation, are these priorities the same or similar to the strategic goals which were set out by the Bosnian Serb leadership on the -- at the 16th session of the Assembly session at the 12th of May? And if not, how do they differ?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several of the points mentioned here are virtually the same as the strategic goals that had been laid out at the 16th session. I would draw the Court's attention to point 2, which says: "The northern border of the Sava River and the breadth of the territory linking the western and eastern part of the Republika Srpska, 20 kilometres wide in its narrowest section between Brcko and Samac." Under point 3, the last paragraph speaks of: "Podgrmec and Potkozarje, from the Una River and the Sava River Basin," and refers to areas that are on the eastern side of the Una river and the southern side of the Sava river. And then number 5, there is no number 4: "The territorial connection between Serbian Sarajevo and the territory of Republika Srpska; and 6) exit to the sea; and 7) border at the Neretva river."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Treanor. Was the Belgrade leadership satisfied with the outcome of Dayton?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Slobodan Milosevic certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what do you base this on?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he gave a speech to the military leadership, the FRY, on the -- at the 47th session of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Rule 65 ter number 06678 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This meeting took place on the 6th of December, 1995, after the conclusion of the Dayton negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 6 of the English translation and page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What did Milosevic say at this meeting, at this session?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on page 6 I would call the Court's attention to the paragraph under Arabic 4, beginning: "Two years ago, the plan of the Contact Group ... at the time when they were keeping 72 per cent of the territory and when they thought that they won the war," they being the Bosnian Serb leadership, "the International Community admitted it and said: 'You can have half the territory of the Bosnia and Herzegovina.' They said that it was unfair on Serbian people," "they" in this case being the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Serb leadership, "although they are 31 per cent of the Serbian people in Bosnia. So 31 per cent of people can get a half of the territory, while 70 per cent of others get the other half of the territory, and it is unfair on those 31 per cent who got a half of the territory. There were some others who had arguments such as: 'Well, Serbs owned 62 per cent of the territory' as if someone would believe it. We know that it was all socially-owned property. The meadows, grazing lands, and mountains were nobody's property. For God sake, what kind of owners are they talking about?"

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Further down on that page, does Mr. Milosevic make reference to the percentage of the square kilometres of land that's been -- that's been achieved?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He talks about how much land the Bosnian Serbs had, in fact, obtained. I could draw the Court's attention to the third paragraph under Roman IV, beginning with "However they destroyed ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Without reading that paragraph, is it possible to summarize for the Chamber what was gained?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he refers to them obtaining 49 per cent of the territory on 25.000 square kilometres in an area where there had never been a Serbian state before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I take you to page 7 of the English translation and page 7 of the B/C/S, does Mr. Milosevic discuss there very briefly the procedures and negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does. He compares it to previous negotiations as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what is the outcome that he says the Bosnian Serbs achieved?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says that the outcome of these negotiations were better than any of the previous maps that had been offered to the Serbs. Toward the bottom of the second paragraph, under Arabic number 5, he said: "This map is the best map for Serbs. They got each town on the Sava River and three towns in the countryside. Then there's the entire Drina River except for Gorazde. It makes 50 towns, 25.000 square kilometres, a half of Bosnia, a republic."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. Mr. Treanor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am, you don't want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, I do, Your Honour. Pages 1 and -- page 1 is actually the agenda, in the English translation at least. Page 1, 2, 6, and 7 of the English translation, and 1, 2, 6 and 7 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, in giving your evidence, you've taken the Trial Chamber to a number of documents in relation to the formation of Serbian entities - the Republic of Serbian Krajina in Croatia, the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You've also taken the Trial Chamber to a number of statements made by the Bosnian Serb leadership and the leadership of the FRY. What, in your opinion, were they attempting --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, we are having trouble with our screens here. The transcript has disappeared, and it says it's attempting to connect with the server.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may. If we may get the technician to come and help, please. Yes, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, what, in your opinion, were the Bosnian Serb and the leadership of the FRY attempting to achieve?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the period that we've been discussing here, in -- very concisely and briefly, what the Serbian leaders were attempting to achieve was that all Serbs be in one state. They were all in one state in the SFRY and the Bosnian Serb leaders, the Croatian Serb leaders, and the leaders in power in Belgrade wished to keep the Serbs living outside of the Republic of Serbia within the FR -- the SFRY, which was in the course of dissolution. It became clear to the leaders in Belgrade, at least at a certain point in time, toward the end of 1991 or beginning of 1992, that given the fact that international recognition was proceeding of the individual republics of Yugoslavia within their existing borders that simply keeping the Serbs in Croatia and the Serbs in Bosnia within Yugoslavia was not going to be possible. They therefore proceeded to the formation of a new state, the FRY, that only included Serbia and Montenegro; however, they supported the efforts of the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia to gain control of territories in those republics that they regarded as Serbian territory, with the ultimate aim of uniting all those territories, that is, the territories in Croatia, Bosnia, and the FRY, at a future date into one state.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that towards the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, but did this -- did this aim continue right the way through until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said at that particular point in time, the idea of simply keeping those territories within the SFRY became not viable in the opinion of the Belgrade leadership, certainly Slobodan Milosevic, so they change tack and, as I said, form the FRY and support of the efforts of Croatia and Bosnia Serbs to gain control of territories in those republics and keep control of those territories over the course of the next few years, with the ultimate goal of uniting all those territories into one state. The -- when that goal would be achieved was never specified precisely. There was talk of five years, ten years, 20 years, at various times, but it was a -- it remained the long-term goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sutherland. Mr. Guy-Smith, you've got four minutes to go to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Shall we go to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why don't we go to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for giving us an extra four minutes. We'll break now and come back at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I'd like to start by talking with you for a moment about your general experience, essentially your CV, if we could.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard I'll be dealing with a document which you supplied, which was your CV. I'm less concerned with each and every part, but I would just like to get a rough understanding, if we could, about some of what could be the salient points with regard to your qualifications as they relate to your testimony here. As I understand it, you were involved in the study of Balkan foreign policy and history; is that correct? And I'm talking about in 1971 and 1972, when you were a special student researching Bulgarian foreign policy.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your studies in the 1970s, did you have occasion to study the political system, the historical area, with regard to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And specifically during that period of time, did you have occasion to study at all the governmental institutions that existed under Mr. Tito?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there came a point in time when you worked as a historian at the United States Department of Justice.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was a number of years after you completed your studies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "completed your studies."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In 1980 you began to work for the United States Department of Justice; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were doing that work, when you were working for the Department of Justice, as I understand it, your work was involved in investigations of litigations of alleged Nazi war criminals that were living in the United States.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was your work at that time involved in the prosecution of such individuals as a matter of -- a criminal matter, or was it a matter of the United States Department of Justice's position with regard to whether they should remain within the United States, residents of the United States?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the latter. The cases were denaturalisation and/or deportation cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those were cases that went through the immigration department?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, which were under civil procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During that period of time, when you were involved in that particular work, were you ever involved in a case where you made a determination that an individual should remain in the country?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my determination to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. But based on the research and investigation you did, did you make a determination that an individual should remain in the country?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made determinations that cases should be closed, that no further action should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And within the 14-year period of time that you were working at the Department of Justice, could you tell me -- could you tell us about how many of those cases you determined should be closed out of the entire number of cases that you were working on, if you could? And I'm not trying to stretch you for figures. If you remember, that's great, but ...

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that's out of how many cases?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any given time I would have, say, a hundred cases assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would this be a couple of dozen out of a hundred or a couple of dozen out of your entire period of employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a good question, Your Honour. Roughly a couple dozen total. You know, the total of number cases ever assigned to me might have risen to 150 or 200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand that. What is the 150 or 200?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total of number that were ever assigned to me over that 13-year period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before you were involved in that work, you were an intelligence analyst working for the Library of Congress, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you were doing that job, that was not a job that was a part of the Department of Justice, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Library of Congress is part of the legislative branch of the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My understanding, okay. Now, during the time that you were engaged as an intelligence analyst, did you produce any papers with regard to your analytic work that were published and reviewed by any of your peers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if you'd like it, I can make it one question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be multi-part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's make it two. Let's make it two. Did you publish papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the answer to the first question obviously takes care of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the second one. And as I understand your language proficiency, you understand Bulgarian, Serbo-Croatian, and Russian in terms of writing and reading -- I'm sorry, in terms of reading -- let me do that again. You understand Bulgarian, Serbo-Croatian, and Russian in terms of reading those languages easily.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to speaking, you speak Bulgarian easily, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You consider yourself fluent in Bulgarian.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was ever quite fluent. I'm a bit rusty perhaps at this point, but I can still speak it easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you can speak it easily, you can speak it to the point of being able to operate as the people who work for us, I take it? And by that I mean interpreters who would be able to engage in simultaneous interpretation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never done simultaneous interpretation in Bulgarian. I've done consecutive translation, but I wouldn't say I was at that level, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to Russian, would you claim that your proficiency in Russian with regard to speaking the language is distinct -- is the same as it is in Bulgarian, or would there be a distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my Russian is probably a little more rusty. I did pass the UN proficiency test in Russian a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That not the case, however, with Serbo-Croatian. Serbo-Croatian is a language, by your own estimation, you don't speak easily. As a matter of fact, you indicated with regard to your proficiency, it's not easily that you speak the language. I'm using the words that you've chosen in your CV; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us for a moment, since we've been dealing a fair amount here with issues concerning the meaning of words, whether or not you believe that a spoken word and a written word obtain the same definition in meaning in the absence of the context in which the word arises?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think any word, whether written or spoken, has a range of meanings, an area of meaning. I think when a word is spoken, the particular meaning that the speaker wishes to impart can be clearer than when it is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your efforts, and specifically your efforts in terms of the work that you have done here, you have been working, as I understand it, from documents in large measure with regard to the report that you compiled for our purposes; correct? Documents.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been involved with documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- broadly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In terms of the report that you compiled for us here, did you have occasion to listen to any audiotapes from which you then made notes or wrote parts of your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I listened to a couple of the audios that we had, for instance, the meeting I think in Banja Luka in the autumn of 1991. We have a transcript of that, and I listened to the audio --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to check the transcripts. I can't remember if there were -- there might have been a couple other videos, videos that I might have looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But in large measure, it would be fair to say that the information upon which you relied was written information.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you have a copy of your report with you, do you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, great. And just so we're clear, that report is in English. It's not in B/C/S, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us earlier that the manner in which you prepared your report is you reviewed selected items that you deemed relevant with regard to the specific request that you received; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by I reviewed selected items. I reviewed items that had been chosen by category for me to review, the category being documents which related to the statements or activities, discussions, of the highest level state and party leaders in the former Yugoslavia. From that group of documents I selected ones that I thought would be relevant to the purpose of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you receive a specific request from the Office of the Prosecutor, from a particular individual, asking you to prepare a report along the lines that you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was that by e-mail or was that orally? How did you get that request?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been Susan Somers; I think Fred Ossogo might have been present at that meeting from the trial team at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So as you recall, it was at a minimum yourself, Susan Somers, and potentially Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. And at that meeting the idea of you preparing a report was discussed, I take it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before we go any further, was that meeting memorialised in any fashion in terms of a memorandum between the parties as to what the general goals or objectives of your report might be?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. During that meeting, could you tell us, if you recall, about how long it was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifteen, 20 minutes. Half an hour, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during that period of time, from 15 minutes to half an hour, whatever it may be, I take it it was a dialogue as between the parties as to what would be important with regard to the report that you were to prepare.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been August 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. After the meeting that you had with Ms. Somers and at least Mr. Ossogo as well, you went about preparing the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at that point you were aware of the fact that you were preparing a report for a particular case, were you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that case was a case that involved the gentleman who sits with us here today, Momcilo Perisic; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the time that you were having this meeting with the Prosecutor and Mr. Ossogo at a minimum, were you discussing what would be the best manner of putting that information together for this report, or was that left in your discretion entirely?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best manner of putting together -- no, I don't think that was a subject of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Did you discuss -- did you discuss in that meeting whether or not in the report you would articulate the extent to which factors such as the breaking of truces by all the parties who were involved would be important for purposes of understanding the contextual and chronological history of, as you've termed it, the leadership during that period?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That subject wasn't mentioned at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What subjects were mentioned in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to write a report about the goals of the Serbian leadership and the extent to which they might have achieved those goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the first request, which is the goals of the Serbian leadership, was that defined for you any more specifically than what you've just told us here?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goals?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mention was made of the setting up of the various entities and the background to those entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "various entities," could you be a bit more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RSK, the RS, and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Was that -- was the suggestion made to you that that be done in a vacuum? And once again, by "a vacuum," what I mean by that is that you would not include or you would include what was happening with other parties, since this was a multi-partied conflict, and to the extent that you were dealing with the issue of what the goals were of the Serbian leadership, one would think you would take into account what other parties, apart from the three that you've just mentioned, were doing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that figured in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did not figure.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What else did figure in the conversation, as you sit here today, apart from the two things that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I sought clarification of what kind of sources generally I should use, that is, documents as opposed to witness testimony in other cases, witness statements, that kind of thing, which I generally do not use, and the response was, yes, you don't need to use that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you asked the question of seeking clarification of sources, generally and specifically, the issue of witness testimony that you just raised us, I take it that you were aware of, at least through that discussion, that there could well be witness testimony that would impact upon the report you were to write; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That there could be, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's because there have been a number of trials here in which some of the same issues that you've discussed with us today have come up; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you've testified in some of those cases; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you, during the discussion that you were having with the Prosecutor, discuss any of the witness testimony that might be germane to your report, whether or not you chose to use it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It was more of a generalised question that you asked in terms of, Should I be looking at witness testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I probably said, I generally don't look at that kind of thing; I hope that's your expectation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you were -- you were at that point reiterating something that's well-known about you, right, Mr. Treanor? I mean, you've been here for a long time.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's well-known about me, but I was reiterating a common point of mine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And they agreed with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you -- did you, at the time that you were talking about writing the report, draw any other requirements or boundaries, and I don't mean that in a restrictive way but rather a positive way, as to how you intended to proceed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I probably went a little bit beyond what they had -- what the -- what the fulfilment of the task would have required, but beyond that I don't think so. What I set out to do is set forth in the introduction to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: When you said you probably went a little bit beyond what they had, I guess you didn't finish that, "they had" being --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they had in mind by the goals of the Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you did that, what did you suggest to them were things that should be thought about in terms of that particular issue, that being the goals of the "Serbian leadership," as we put it? I'm putting that in quotations because there are quite a different number of people who are involved in that particular statement, "Serbian leadership." As you've told us here, we have three distinct governments, whether or not they're formally recognised or not, as well as a myriad of other people. So when you made that suggestion to them, what did you say to them in that regard, in terms of what they hadn't thought about and perhaps they should think about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I said anything in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what did you -- where did you go a little bit beyond what they had thought about?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there's a section in here on the JNA or the military, the Yugoslav Army and the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia, I thought that would be useful. I probably went through the negotiating process further than might have been imagined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those are things that you suggested to them would be points that would potentially be germane to the discussion of the Bosnian leadership, as you've termed it in your report, before you wrote the report, that is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So what you did, then, if I understand it, is you independently made a determination that these are areas that should be included in the report above and beyond that which you discussed in this meeting in August of 2006.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that would be fair to say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, fine. I wasn't there. You did what you did, and I'm just trying to get an understanding so the Chamber has an understanding of how you went about preparing the report. Now, you told us that when you prepare the report, what you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. My apologies to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you prepare the report, is that you do so with a body of, as I understand it, some 31.000, give or take, source documents that you have in your library --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry for interrupting. Can I have a page number for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've just misplaced one of my binders, and I will get you the page. We'll get back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that when you're compiling the report, the report, as it's compiled, is done as best you can, and the most important constraint -- the most important problem that you have, if I'm putting it properly, is that the report of this nature takes place within the context of certain constraints, the most important being time and space. And that's at page 914; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to this report, you were operating under that particular dilemma of time and space; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And specifically, I'd like to spend a moment on the issue of time, which is you were under a time constraint; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you had to get the report done in a couple of months; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was less than two months. It was a month and a half, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us exactly when you started writing the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not off the top of my head, Your Honour. I think I started the end of August, and the date on the original report was 11 October, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So that was the constraint that you had in terms of time --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- is you had to get the report done by the 11th of October, 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, between --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do have a concern about this date of October 11th, 2006. When you say "original report," was there a subsequent report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the report before us now is a corrected version of the original report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Let me not interfere with your examination, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- in terms of the time constraints - and I want to spend a moment there - since the report was filed on the 11th of October, 2006, did you have occasion at that time -- let me put it to you in other terms. When you finished the report, were you satisfied that the report was as accurate and complete as possible, given your time constraints?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You felt that this report was obviously ready for prime time; otherwise, you wouldn't have delivered it to the Prosecutor for purposes of it being published as a document upon which they would rely and a document upon which the Defence would review; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Getting back to the length constraint, I mean, as I think I indicated earlier, the -- part of the request was that it be kept short.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the question that my colleague asked, it's at page 908. "We now have a collection of 31.000 separate issues of newspapers and magazines," is what I was referring to in terms of the figure, and that's at page 908, line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since we're on that just for the moment, I take it that the 31.000 separate issues of newspapers and magazines does not include some of the documents we've been discussing here today and during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is only a portion of the collection of material that was available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So, in fact, it was over 31.000 documents that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the issue of putting your report together, did you make a determination as you were putting the report together that certain things should be omitted from the report? There was certain information that was not necessarily relevant to the task at hand.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the constraints of space at that point, one tries to convey the substance of the document as briefly as possible. The paragraphs of the report are basically summaries of relevant portions of documents, so a summary is a summary. Backing up a step, of course, there's the issue of selection of which documents to use, and it's impossible to use them all so I chose the ones which, in my estimation, were the most relevant of the ones available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you chose the ones that, in your view -- I'm sorry, in your estimation, were the most relevant of the ones available to you, do you take into account, in terms of a methodology of putting your report together, any hypothetical presumptions or objective structures? Let me give you, for example, what I'm referring to because it might be of some assistance, which is did you take into account any of the notions behind such a hypothetical theory as game theory, which is the study of strategic interactions among rationale players which produce outcomes with respect to preferences of those players, which is something that I think has been used in the area of international conflicts.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take conscious account of that theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you are aware of the fact that there has been literature, and a fair amount of literature, produced and published concerning the application of game theory to international conflicts, are you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You do not find that to be necessarily a theory that you would want to apply in a situation where you were dealing with an international conflict and you were dealing with multiple parties, and you were asked a question concerning goals over a period of some years? That seemed to you not to be something worth consideration.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't even occur to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Have you heard about or have any awareness of theories concerning, once again, in the area of inter-state crises what are called audience costs?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the notion, once again, in terms of the methodology to be applied to a conflict situation, that in an audience-cost theory, there's an analysis of inter-state bargaining, and one of the things they take into account, of course, is the relatively -- relative military might of participants and the willingness of each side to use force in order to demonstrate a higher degree of commitment to the issue at stake than the opponent? Did you take that into account?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That, as a matter of fact, is one of the things that was occurring in the conflict that you were looking at; correct? Apart from saber-rattling, there was also, in fact, actual use of military force.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was use of military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you heard of the term, once again in terms of that particular scientific methodology of approaching a problem, the notion of what is called "competitions in risk-taking"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have heard such a thing, but I'm not familiar with the theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you're not familiar with the theory, then obviously it’s not something you applied for purposes of the report that you wrote. And obviously from what we've seen, you did not apply any statistical models whatsoever to a determination of the goals that existed for this period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, what you did do is you picked documents that you, as I understand it, determined were relevant to the issue at hand; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us already, and that was in the discussions that you had your first day, and I'm referring to page 917, that there's an element of subjectivity or an ideological approach that exists and that existed in the creation of this particular report; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said there's always such elements present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, such elements were present when you wrote this particular report; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough.
