I mean -- and, in a certain sense, the report is not value-free or neutral, and by "neutral" I mean neutral from the standpoint as we don't have objective information upon which we can gauge if the conclusion that you've reached, and I'm referring to the conclusion that you reached at the very end of your testimony here today most importantly, is an accurate conclusion, number 1, or is the only conclusion, number 2, that could be reached based upon the documents that you reviewed; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I reached that conclusion in the report. I don't think there is any conclusion in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a selection of documents that would bear on that issue. People -- you're entirely correct. Different people, different readers, could draw different conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that would -- that defeats, the ability to draw different conclusions defeats one of the purposes, at least from the standpoint of a methodology, does it not? And by that I mean, generally speaking, when creating a report, the idea, among others, is that somebody entirely different, a new person, could take that same information that you used and come up with the same conclusions; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm a historian, and one of the highest form of praise for a work of history is that, Well, I don't agree with his conclusions, but he's presented enough material to enable the reader to form alternate conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And would it be fair to say that when you wrote this report that you were, maybe at least subconsciously, interested in that highest form of praise. And I don't mean that on a personal level, but in terms of an effort, when you wrote the report, you wrote the report so that one could obtain a different conclusion from the conclusion that you you've reached here today based upon the body of the information that you have presented to us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I presented the material that I thought were relevant -- was relevant to the consideration of that issue and leave it up to the reader to draw whatever conclusion or types of conclusions the reader wishes to draw on -- on the matters discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that's based upon your perception of what your role is, I take it, in writing the report; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is that the report is to be objective; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Complete; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is complete as the various constraints permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Balanced; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And fair, fair in its assessment to all of the considerations that would revolve around that report; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could hardly be the case, all the considerations that revolve around the report, as I state in the introduction to the report, this is not a history of the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia, so all the considerations that revolve around the report are not included in -- could hardly have been included, certainly not within the constraints of 60 pages or something that was initially given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. As a matter of fact, do you believe that with regard to this report, that you applied a universal set of rules concerning minimal standards of a scientifically objective piece?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've mentioned on a couple of occasions that if you'd been given more time and space, it would have been much more complete or longer; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you finished this report on the 11th of October, 2006, approximately two years and a month ago, give or take -- maybe today, maybe it's two years and a month exactly, give or take a day; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that two years that have transpired since you wrote the report, considering your concern about the constraints that you had with regard to time, did you make any efforts to modify, amend, edit, or add to the report that you felt may have suffered as a result of the time constraints that you were placed under?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I started on that right away, but the -- my objective was not to rewrite the report; it was simply to correct some of the deficiencies that -- editorial deficiencies, of the report; namely, supplying ERN numbers of documents that did not have ERNs at the time the report was written, correcting typographical errors. I eliminated a couple of things that were based on documents that I decided were not reliable for the purpose I was using them. So it's a corrected -- editorially corrected version of the report that I was working on. I was not working on rewriting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You were satisfied, then, that -- let me rephrase that. When you engaged in the corrections - and I'm using that term in a generic sense - that you just discussed with us, you, as a matter of fact, reduced the report in this number of paragraphs by two, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it wasn't any longer, as you've told us, than it would be had you been given more time. It wasn't any longer.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the amendments that you made to the report are, quite frankly - and I mean this in a positive, not a negative with regard to the report - are, quite frankly, de minimus.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When did you do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I indicated I started doing that fairly soon after the original report was filed, and I completed that on the 1st of September, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So the deletion of two paragraphs, as you've told us, putting in some appropriate ERN numbers, and, as I understand it, you have actually moved some of the paragraphs around --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. I think actually there are six paragraphs that you changed in the report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly. Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a letter from the Prosecutor that indicates that. And I'm not asking you to say that's absolutely accurate or inaccurate. But I received an indication that you made some very slight amendments.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, a very slightly amended version. Now, I take it you started working on that immediately after the final was filed in October of 2006, and the efforts that you put into that, that's what took some two years for purposes of, as you've told us here, had you had the time, you would have given us a more complete and longer report; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't work on it every day, all day, for two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, no, I'm sure you didn't.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it took two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to the introduction of your report, Mr. Treanor, paragraph 5, as I read it, you indicated that "the primary purpose of such a description," and the description you're referring to is the one that's contained in paragraph 4, "is to facilitate a realistic and accurate understanding of the larger context in which it is alleged that the Serbian leadership was involved in massive violations of international humanitarian law in BH and Croatia, and to identify the individuals who fill the highest level military and civilian positions within the Serbian entities." Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I don't recall hearing in the description that you gave us that what the purpose of your report was what is written in paragraph 5, and perhaps you could help us. Going back to that meeting that you had in August of 2006, during that meeting, was one of the things that you discussed as a primary purpose of the report that you wrote what I just read to you? Because that certainly would be distinct from that which you have told us thus far.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I may have expanded a bit on what was -- what I was asked to do, and I sat down and, when I was done, wrote this introduction and thought about, What is it I'm doing here, and set -- set out that paragraph, which I think is one I've used in other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether you've used it in other reports or not is irrelevant, sir. Is it your testimony here that with regard to that particular paragraph -- and apparently, since you've used it in other reports, I take it, that it must have been something that you did discuss at the meeting that you had with the Prosecutor with regard to what the purpose of your endeavours were to be.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly not point A. I think something around point B might have come up, the idea of -- again, laying out the development of the entities and with that, who the office-holders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why do you reject point -- why do you reject point A and say to us certainly not, when you've indicated that this is a paragraph that you've used in previous reports? And I take it that it would be fair to say that in the conversation that you had with the Prosecution in August, one of the things that you discussed was whether there was an awareness of those previous reports that you had written.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that that came up in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, in the same fashion that you've alluded to what you considered to be the awareness of others who may not have been present, could you tell us whether or not the individuals who were involved in that initial meeting, and by that I mean Ms. Somers and Mr. Ossogo at a minimum, were aware of your reports, had read your reports?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had read all my reports. They all hadn't been written perhaps at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, let's be -- let's be honest here now. You are an in-house, as you put it, historian for the Office of the Prosecutor; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have been here for many years; true?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you are, as I understand it, a team leader of a highly sophisticated group of people that are involved in investigating and culling information which is used by the Office of the Prosecutor to prosecute those people who appear at this Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a team leader, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you rejecting the fact that you have a sophisticated team? Because if you are, then I'll delete that from my question.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, once again I'm going to ask you the same question, which is: You're involved in investigating and culling information. You've told us you engage in a selection process when you write those reports, so you cull information; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "cull." Perhaps you could define that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Select information which is used by the Office of the Prosecutor to prosecute people who appear at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we select information. Whether it all gets used in a prosecution is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many reports have you written, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I think four altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what the fate of those four reports is with regard to whether or not they've been used or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two of them have been used in trials. There's another one that was submitted for a trial -- in connection with a trial that hasn't begun yet, and then there would be this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is pending.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So in your experience of those reports that you have authored or that you have been responsible for a team authoring, they have been used for purposes of prosecuting individuals who appear before this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they do not encompass all the information that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did not ask you that question, did I?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that to be the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence actually asked Mr. Treanor whether -- whether Ms. Somers and Mr. Ossogo had read the reports. That's where we were going about a page ago. And Mr. Treanor said that he wasn't aware. And then Mr. Guy-Smith said, Well, let's be honest here, and I should have stood up at that point, but the fact of the matter is simply because they are used in other cases doesn't mean that other trial teams have read those reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an objection, or what is it, ma'am? Is it an argument?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just objecting to the tone of Mr. Guy-Smith's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The tone? What tone, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He's just conflating. He starts off by saying, Have these people read these reports, and then, let's be honest, you're an in-house expert, and then goes into what the fate of the reports are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How would you like him to do it, ma'am? I understand you would like to prescribe to Mr. Guy-Smith how he should conduct his cross-examination. How would you like him to do it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was the tone that he was using in relation to the questions that there was no basis for the tone in the way that the question had been answered. It didn't relate to -- the earlier question was simply had Ms. Somers and Mr. Ossogo read the report, and then he completely changes around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, your objection is overruled. I can't even ask for a response from the opposite side because I don't understand what you're talking about. Carry on, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many people were on your team? And I have two separate questions here, so let me tell you what I'm interested in understanding here because it may be easier to do it in one or not, which is how many people are on your team, and how many people who are on your team were involved in the writing of this report, or the supplying of information to you about this particular report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, currently there are, I believe, 20 people on the team, including myself and interns. The number of people that may have contributed to this report is, I think, impossible for me to say, since, as I indicated, much of the material that I -- on the basis of which I made my selection was found in our CaseMap, and any number of people, a large number of people, put things into the CaseMap. So I can't say how many people contributed to that. As I indicated at one point, I believe, I have -- or under my direction people have gone methodically through various categories of high level state and party documents and entered them into the CaseMap so that it would be a very large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you have a number of people who methodically enter the documents into CaseMap --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, methodically review and then the material is entered into CaseMap, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you have an internal quality control system for that entry into CaseMap that you use?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And do you personally review the source material for all of the entries of the 31.000 newspapers and articles, plus all the oodles of other information that you have, to make a determination as to whether or not the information that is contained in your CaseMap is, using a term I used before, "spot-on" accurate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all of the 31.000 items are entered into the CaseMap, but I certainly do personally review what has been put in there and review the documents, especially when it comes to a re-review when it comes to producing a report of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this report, this specific report, is a report that, I use the word "penned," because I actually began a life before there were computers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So this is a report that was penned by you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In its entirety. This is your report. There are no other authors to this report but you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except insofar as something in CaseMap might have been entered by someone else and found its way into this report. But I reviewed everything, and I'm responsible for everything that's in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were asked to prepare this report, did you have CaseMap then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you told us beforehand about the distinction between writing the drafts and the CaseMap, this is a report that was written with the utilisation of CaseMap; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Can you give us some assistance, and I know that some questions were asked of you initially both by Judge Moloto and Judge David concerning the objective criteria that you used in selecting not only the documents but the portions of the documents that you've submitted to us here. What were your criteria? Do you have a list of those criteria? Do you have a spreadsheet of those criteria?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are those criteria that are to be found somewhere in the recesses of your own thinking?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's where they're to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do those -- are those criteria in a constant? Do they change?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean over the course of the six or seven weeks I was writing the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, I sort of expanded on -- in certain respects to a strict interpretation of elucidating the goals of the Serbian leadership and the establishment of their structures, so to that extent -- but on the primary issue which was the goals of the Serbian leadership, I would say that remained constant and, as I've said before, I selected items and portions of items which I thought were relevant or most relevant to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I know you've said "relevant" and "most relevant," so obviously you're going through some kind of shading process here or --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for instance, we have speeches by Slobodan Milosevic. I picked out those portions of the speeches that I thought most succinctly captured the main idea of the speech insofar as it was relevant to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do I understand it that with regard, and I'm generalising here for the moment, and I'm sure we'll talk about this more fully, that what you found relevant in terms of Slobodan Milosevic's speeches were, one, that he was constantly from, I believe as you said, the end of 1991 forward pressing for some kind of peace settlement. That was one of the things that you found to be relevant; right? Because you've talked to us about this a fair amount?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it's in there, yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you chose the speeches, sir, so I'm asking you a direct question. You found those to be relevant?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to -- and that's one of a number of things. Obviously, there are other things that you found to be relevant, too. That's one of the things you found to be relevant. With regard to the sources that you used, as I understand it, your source material came from records of a variety of different governmental bodies, and I'm putting it in a generic term, first of all; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It includes those types of records.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. That's one of a series. And the governmental bodies that you looked at included the RS; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, if that's what you mean by "government body," yes. Entity, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Entity. Well, and it also included the RSK; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the RS is the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The RSK is the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It included FRY; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. And FRY is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those are three -- for purposes of your presentation to us here, those are three separate, as you've put it, entities, separate political entities, whether or not, once again, they were recognised being a different matter, that had fully formed, over the period of your report, had fully formed governments; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And they all had constitutions; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They all had in their constitutions provisions for armies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They all had armies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also, apart from those particular documents and entities, you also have information for particular political parties; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, you've discussed with us a bit about that, mainly in terms of the political party that Mr. Karadzic was involved in before he became part of the Presidency, and I want to make sure I'm using the proper term, the Presidency of the republic; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He continued to be involved with that party after he became president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in addition, you analysed for purposes of the report speeches and platforms and positions that were taken by Mr. - and I always pronounce his name poorly, so you can help me, I'm sure - Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Izetbegovic. You analysed his positions, did you not, and his party's positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, with regard to the issue of understanding in some kind of context, a goal, would you agree with me that it's important to see how the various participants who may be involved in what I'm going to call here in the broadest sense "a conflict" act and respond?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would get more toward writing a history of the conflicts, rather than examining the goals of the Serbian leaders and how they sought to achieve them. I, as a general matter, take your point, but I think that would go beyond the scope of what I was asked to do and certainly result in a product of much greater length.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which, had you had the time, you could have done because you told us that before.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, because I was asked to produce a report of about 60 pages, I believe, and I think this is 75 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. So being an individual in the position that you are, do I understand it that you were not in a position, if you felt that you needed more space to create a fuller picture, that you were disallowed that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was given certain parameters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What were the parameters that you were given?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty pages; October the 20th. Those were the parameters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: October the 20th of what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2006. I think that was the deadline for the submission of expert reports in this case. At that time, that is, in August 2006, when this request was made of me, I was already scheduled to go on home leave in October so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. You've answered my question. That's fine. October 2006. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're not suggesting, are you, here that for the years 1990 to 1995, during the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, that the goals were static? Are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. This was a very, very, very dynamic situation; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a dynamic situation, yes. How many "verys" it requires, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps I have one "very" too many. But this was at the time of conflict that engaged the entire whole world at some level, diplomatically, economically, politically; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly occupied the international community. Whether it was the entire world --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's what I meant by -- that's what I meant by "the entire world."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll then take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your tenure here, sir, you have learned, among other things, about the participant -- participation of various groups and individuals in the conflict, obviously.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to direct your attention just for a moment, if I could, once again with always in mind the notion of how does one gauge what a goal is and how does one gauge what is appropriate in making a determination of what somebody's goal is, an individual whose name is Mr. Izetbegovic. Now, could you tell us who he was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, I believe you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was the head of the Party of Democratic Action in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a Muslim party. He was elected to the Presidency of the SR BiH in December 1990 as a Muslim member of that Presidency. The seats on the Presidency were allotted by ethnicity, and he was elected President of the Presidency by other members of the Presidency toward the end of December 1990. He continued in that position throughout the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before 2003, if I understand your state of knowledge with regard to this particular individual, you knew that he had been imprisoned in Yugoslavia under the Tito regime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under the Tito regime in 2003?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, in 2003, Mr. Treanor was aware of the fact that Mr. Izetbegovic had been imprisoned under the Tito regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You were not aware, at least before October 15th, that he had been imprisoned for circulation of a document called "The Islamic declaration," which he wrote in 1970. If I could refresh your recollection, you were asked some questions by Mr. Ackerman in this regard, and you indicated that you were not aware of the fact that he had been imprisoned for that particular writing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I may not have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What year are we talking about? October the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. After the cross-examination that you were involved in with Mr. Ackerman in which this issue came up, did you educate yourself with regard to his particular views, and I don't mean Mr. Ackerman's, I mean Mr. Izetbegovic's views, as they related to being a fundamentalist Muslim?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already read "The Islamic Declaration" at that point. I don't think I read anything else about that matter after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you factor into your analysis of how the various parties were responding to each other, the position that he had, the political position that he had, and the doctrine that he espoused, as it related to the goals, as you've termed them, of the Bosnian Serb leadership, since he was a principal player, was he not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And his attitudes and the views he espoused clearly impacted upon the reactions of and the goals, as you've put them, that the Serbian leadership would have, would they not? There would be an inter-play as between those two.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to your examination of the historical record, once again, we're not dealing with any one of these parties in a vacuum, are we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "dealing." No. Generally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report focuses on the Serbian leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But with regard -- with regard to what your report focuses on, there is an underlying component part, I'm suggesting to you, that one would think would be taken into account, and that is how those goals came about, and by that I mean what was the inter-play between the various parties and now, for just a moment, I'm speaking with regard to Mr. Izetbegovic, because he espoused a particular political reality, did he not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what political reality -- reality he espoused at any particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by a "political reality."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In 1990, when he was -- when he was coming into power, he made it very clear what his views were with regard to what should happen in that particular area, did he not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm familiar with the programme of his party --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the programme of his party in that period?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recollect the relevant portion, they spoke about Bosnia remaining within the SFRY if other republics also remained within the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that would be at that point in time, at least initially, that would be a position which was consistent with, for example, Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Because at that point in time there was a -- there was a -- in 1990, there was, in fact, actually -- I'm trying to think of a term that encompasses it without attributing any blame or fault to anyone. There was the beginnings of a true crisis in the making as to what was going to happen to a region that had enjoyed a form of unity for some number of years; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. There came a point in time when his position shifted, and by that I mean remaining in the SFRY if everyone else decided to remain in the SFRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that did change. What did change was that other people decided they didn't want to remain in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to his particular -- and just for the minute, I know we're deviating from what the specific report that you wrote says, but just for the moment, with regard to his particular goal at that time in 1990, which was to remain in the SFRY, it shifted because of something that occurred: Other areas decided not to remain within the SFRY, specifically, if I'm not mistaken, Slovenia and Croatia. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But his goal -- the SDA goal stated originally, I believe, included that contingency, because, as you said, this process was underway, and it was more or less recognised that certain republics may choose to leave the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, at the point in time that that was occurring, that there was a recognition that certain republics may choose to leave the SFRY, there was a fair amount of concern of what the effect of such a breakup would be; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just talking generally here for the moment. And at that point -- and at that point in time in 1990, one of the -- one of the concerns was that, for the moment what I'm going to call a nation state, and I don't know whether you agree with me that's an appropriate term, so I want to make sure that we have our terms -- we're agreed on terms, a nation state, that being Yugoslavia, was going to now potentially become a series of independent units, political units.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there was a great deal of concern over the issue of how internal boundaries were going to be drawn, if they could be drawn.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that point in time, within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mean, that had not yet reached the point of becoming an international question, had it, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. When did it become an international question?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think by the middle of 1991, the international community was pretty well occupied with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And "that issue" being the issue of the propriety of there being internal boundaries drawn in the former nation -- well, let me take that back. The propriety of internal boundaries being drawn in the nation state of Yugoslavia, because it still was, for all intents and purposes, politically recognised as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, they became occupied with the issue of the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, and that was certainly one of the important issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And you've discussed with us issues concerning a variety of different terms that were being used as to whether or not there would be independent nations, whether there would be a co-federation, whether there would be federated states, a variety of different terms.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A lot of what was occurring, at least at the early time, was a struggle to figure out what was going to occur in terms of what had been a single-nation state; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A single state. I would object to the term "nation state," I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I'll use that. I'll use "single state." I want to make sure that here we're definitely speaking the same language. I don't want to be off your thinking because you've read most of the documents. Now, what area was the first area to proclaim that it was going to remove itself from the state?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are matters of definition, but I think generally Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how did they go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over a period of months, they adopted a number of amendments to their constitution, referendums, and then eventually on the 25th of June, 1991, they declared independence and sought to assert control over the borders -- the external borders of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say they sought to exert control over the external borders of Slovenia, those borders, the Slovenian borders, were borders that had been here to for recognised as part of the Slovenian republic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, but they were also the external borders of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And what you had up until that point in time is, as I recall, was you had -- is you had six constituent republics and two autonomous or three autonomous provinces that made up the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Two autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So that would not be dissimilar, if we were just to use a parallel notion, that would not be dissimilar to the United States, would it, where we have 50 states, and then we have, what I will call for the moment, a couple of autonomous provinces, or at least one, that being Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wouldn't be a very good analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't like that analysis.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Forgetting about Puerto Rico, what do you think about it with regard to just the notion of the 50 states and the six constituent republics making up a single state.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fairly good analogy. I realise there are technicalities of constitutional law which I couldn't possibly comment on, but, yes, we have two federations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the reason you couldn't possibly comment on them is because that would require some legal interpretation and constitutional interpretation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Which is outside of your specific area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Certainly comparing the constitutions of two states --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, no, I mean, it's hard enough to do it within the United States, let alone something like we're talking about here. Now, when Slovenia declared its, as you put it, and as I think they did, their independence, the way that they did that is they went through a referendum process. They voted.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there were a series of votes that occurred; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how many occurred in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But yes, there was referendum -- there was at least one referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so the conclusion of the referendum process was that the newly formed government of Slovenia was able to say, Our people have voted, and based upon their voting, we declare our independence. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the basic idea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Which is the same thing that happened with regard to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when did they do that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I mentioned that, I might have confused the date, I think it was in May 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Croatian declaration of independence and the Slovenian declaration of independence occurred relatively within a short time of each other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, virtually on the same day, within a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. There then became a concern, did there not, that Bosnia-Herzegovina was planning on going the same route. It was going to be the next area that found itself independent, or was going to attempt to gain independence.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean by "concern," but there was certainly that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the time that there was that idea, one of the things that occurred, did it not, is that the SFRY, which still existed, requested international intervention and assistance with regard to the issue of the propriety of internal boundaries being drawn in this particular manner, whether or not Slovenia had the right to do this, whether or not Croatia had the right to do this.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- I'm aware that they -- someone in Belgrade, the Government of Serbia or -- I think it was the Government of Serbia, actually, requested an opinion from the Badinter Commission about the self-determination of the Serbs. The international community had, I believe, already adopted the position that no borders were to be changed by force, certainly. But I think the specific issue that the Serbian government -- that the Government of Serbia requested guidance on was self-determination for the Serbs in Bosnia and Croatia, which is -- gets to the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned the Badinter Commission. Now, is the Badinter Commission is a commission that was created before or after or during the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had no -- way before the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Way before the Vance-Owen Plan; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And as a matter of fact, the Badinter Commission, at the time that it was engaged in its works, there was some discussion about whether or not the European Commission was going to recognise any of these, I'm going to call them countries for the moment or states, whether they were going to be recognised because there were some concerns about the whole notion of secession from the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was discussion within the EC about the conditions under which the independence of individual republics, might be a good word --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect word.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- could be recognised by member states of the EC.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there was some concern at that point in time, was there not, and please correct me if I'm wrong, about the premature recognition of a republic by Germany specifically as being a potential precipitous act into creating further problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which republic, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, and Croatia, all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Then it should be "republics."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. There was concern about what impact of the recognition of the independence of those republics might have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's right. And specifically there was concern with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina being recognised as a republic before there had been an appropriate referendum process. The premature recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be something that could occur -- something that would result in conflict; correct? And there was an argument back and forth, as a matter of fact, between Mr. Genscher and Mr. de Cuellar at the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who was having which arguments, but there certainly was concern about that, as there had been about Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of your report, did you factor in these particular concerns and events when making a determination of the relevant documents as they related to the Bosnian Serb leadership between 1990 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I included in the report the resolutions of the SR BH Assembly in October that, in effect -- in effect, in my view, declared independence, and I think in the Serbs' view as well, the Bosnian Serbs' view, and I think I mentioned the Badinter Commission decisions in -- certainly in January and the mention of the -- raising the idea of a referendum in BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, the whole idea of the referendum in BH became central to a determination of how that particular area was going to be able to signal its independence, because there had been a vote, and there had been some questions about that vote; right? The first referendum.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "the first referendum."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Badinter Commission made a determination that the initial referendum was not sufficient for purposes of recognition of BH as an independent republic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what referendum they might have been referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they said that whatever had been presented to them was not a sufficient basis for recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that particular determination, the determination that whatever was presented to them was not a sufficient basis for recognition, did you take that particular event, that particular factual event, as something that was a causative factor with regard to the Bosnian Serb goals between the period of time that you've discussed in your report? And obviously this would be after 1990 because the Badinter Commission pronounced after 1990.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean. I lay out in the report, again, documents and portions of documents which I think were relevant to a consideration of that issue. I have documents about the referendum in there and the -- I believe, the Serbs' position in regard to that referendum, as well as about their own plebiscite earlier. I didn't get into issues of causality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By January, before the Badinter Commission report in question, the Bosnian Serbs had already proclaimed their own republic and were proceeding in January to devise a constitution for that republic, as well as work out other issues connected with its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, the Bosnian Serbs took the same course of conduct that had been taken by -- and by that, I'm talking about the referendum and attempting to establish the government, took the same source of conduct that had been undergone by Slovenia and Croatia. Different conditions but same source of conduct; voting and establishing government. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not entirely correct. The referendums in Slovenia and Croatia that we've been discussing were republic-wide referendums. They were not of the type that Mr. Milosevic had been advocating; namely, referendums of peoples, the issue being which peoples wanted to stay in Yugoslavia or leave Yugoslavia. The Bosnian Serbs had conducted what they called a plebiscite in November. It was a Serbian plebiscite. Other people could vote, but it was basically a Serbian plebiscite; I think it was even called that. And the idea was to determine whether the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to remain within Yugoslavia, which they did overwhelmingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you raised there, I think, somewhat of an interesting distinction between the two forms of voting. One is, as you put it, a republic-wide referendum, and if I'm understanding you correctly, the republic-wide referendum would be in conformity with, and I'm sure you know better than I do, a Westfalian notion of state, which is that a state is a unit that has specific boundaries which are, as you defined, the republic-wide boundaries within Slovenia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a conflict here between two different concepts of the state and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And one concept is as I've said the Westfalian concept of state, which has the recognised boundaries, and the other concept is a concept of a state as it relates to peoples.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I think the notion opposed to that, as it was stated at that time, was a civic state, as opposed to a state of peoples. In other words, a civic state in which each citizen is equal and would have an equal vote, as opposed to each of the recognised constituent peoples in the republic, let's get back to that term, in BH would have collective rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The term that you've -- I don't want to say the term. The notion that you've just put forth about collective rights, that was a notion which resonated in the SFRY, and by that I mean the SFRY in reality was a multi-ethnic, multi-religious, multi-peopled society, in which there were some form of checks and balances under what I understand in -- once again, I'm sure you understand it better than I, the key system, although the key system did not necessarily have the checks and balances that you or I would understand from the United States. But there was a form of equality of protection and representation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, the referendums that occurred in both Slovenia and Croatia were antithetical to that principle that had existed within that particular region, within the SFRY, for some 40 or so years; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs certainly saw it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And therein lies, really, in many senses, kind of the nub of the problem. Am I correct in that regard? In terms of the view of how best to have a political entity, a state, in which the people are both -- both have obligations as well as protections and representation, that's really what the fight came to. Right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, in the report I mentioned the new Croatian constitution which had left the Serbs out as one of the constituent nations and their reaction to that situation. So that's precisely the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard -- with regard to that particular issue, that is in -- and I'm not trying to simplify obviously something, which is extremely complex, but that particular issue, the issue of how best to define those protections and that representation, is an issue that resonated throughout the period of 1991 through 1995, if not even further, but certainly during the period of time that your report was addressing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that after the establishment of the RSK and the RS and the FRY, that particular issue receded a bit into the background. Of course, a lot of the focus of the negotiations centred around BH, or the international negotiations centred on the nature of BH and how it would be formed. But it was fairly generally accepted by all the parties in those negotiations that there would, in fact, be separate entities within BH for each of the constituent nations of BH, so that precisely --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- precisely so resolve that issue. But, as I say, it seemed to be accepted that that would be the structure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- rather than a unitary structure which is something that the Serbs didn't want, and Alija Izetbegovic, in his heart of hearts, I think, wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which was a unitary structure.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the goal of the Serbian leadership based upon the discussion that we've just had, would it be fair to say, based upon the documents that you certainly have gone through, that there was a continued attempt to achieve some form of protection for an equality of, whether it was appropriate -- whether it was appropriate or not, the Serbian people who were living in that area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't entirely understand the question. I think the answer is going to be yes, but could you define the area and the time period more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Well, I'm now -- I'm moving into 1992, obviously. And from 1992 onward until 1995, during that period of time, the efforts were for the Serbian leadership, as you've -- and you framed it as a collective, and we'll talk about that a little bit later, but was to obtain for those people equality and protection, are the terms that I used. Whether it would be through the formation of a single state, a number of states, whatever the political entities were, that was what the driving goal was during that entire period of time, ultimately achieved perhaps in a different -- in a different permutation from that which had been international envisioned, based on the concept of people that we talked about earlier, constituent people.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think equality and protection within the framework of the Serbs having their own entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And that in and of itself, the Serbs having their own entities, was a constant sticking point, obviously, because the nature of the entity, the size of the entity, the structure of the entity, is something that, obviously from the documents that we've gone through, has been -- was long and hard fought, argued over, throughout the period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those issues were. As I say, I think the idea that they were going to have their own entities of whatever description was, by that time, generally accepted, and in Bosnia that would mean that the other two constituent nations would have their own entity with whatever relations they chose to have. These entities would -- well, for instance, Republika Srpska defined itself as a state of the Serbian people, so there was only one constituent people in that entity, and that was the framework that had been accepted, fairly generally accepted, for dealing with the situation in Bosnia as a whole. And, as you said, there are these other issues that provoked a lot of discussion as to how to implement that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to turn for a moment, if I could, to your report. And just in terms of dealing with the issue of completeness, accuracy, and choices made - and I refer you and counsel to paragraph 225. Do you have that before you, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 225 you indicate that: "The UNSC condemned the bombardment of Zagreb and other centres of civilian population by the forces of local Serb authorities and demanded their immediate cessation." Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you have a footnote for that with regard to where that information came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 6830, page number 1. My understanding is that there has been no B/C/S translation of this document which is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you, by -- is it up for you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to -- is that the document -- first of all, is that the document from which you gleaned the information that is contained in paragraph 225?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And specifically, the information that you gleaned as being important for purposes of this report is the information which is contained on, I believe it's page 2 of the document. And looking at the second -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the B/C/S translation is actually coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We have seen it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I note that out of the report or not contained in the report is the language that it "calls upon the parties, in particular the Government Of Croatia, to cease all military action in and around Sector South."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That language from that document is not in paragraph 225.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it was your determination, based upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. What you have just read, where is it on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's on page 1 -- excuse me. There always seems to be a problem between paper and e-court. It's paragraph 4 of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Starting --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- on page 1. One, two, three, right there. Going from the top, one, two, three, four: "The Security Council condemns the incursions into the zone of separation by the force of the Government of the Republic of Croatia in Sectors North and South, and by both sides in Sector East. It demands that the forces in question withdraw immediately."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you say what about that paragraph in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That particular paragraph is not contained in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that he does adduce in paragraph 225 of his report, the information that he gives us is the next paragraph, which is: "The Security Council also condemns the bombardment of Zagreb and other centres of civilian population ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the drafting of this particular report, I take it, based upon the information you've given us previously, that you made a determination that that particular pronouncement by the Security Council, the condemnation of a group that was directly involved and impacts upon, generally speaking, the Bosnian Serb leadership's policies was not relevant.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't entirely understand the question. But when it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me put it to you more simply, then: You made a determination that that particular information, the information that the Security Council condemned the incursions by the Government of the Republic of Croatia and demanded the forces in question withdraw immediately, was not relevant for your report.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that information is pretty much contained in paragraph 223.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Could you tell us why you didn't include it with regard to this particular paragraph, since you are citing us to a footnote that has within it this particular information?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this statement was issued only three days later, and the new element here, I felt, was the position that the Security Council was taking in connection with the bombardment of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, interestingly enough, in paragraph 223, there's no issue with regard to the United Nations Security Council's condemnation of the Republic of Croatia. It's a demand; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there's a distinction, is there not, in those documents that you have reviewed, sir, between a demand and a condemnation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I think a demand is stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, I'd like to spend a moment on some chronology and see if you could be of some help to us, if you could. I believe that you have told us that on May 12th, 1992, a couple of relatively important events occurred, one of them being the constitution of the Republika Srpska, specifically with a recognition of the Presidency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the constitutional law of what became known as Republika Srpska, at that time was known as the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the constitutional law that was in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it was both. There were also amendments to the constitution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On that day the Presidency was elected; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, pursuant to the amendment of the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Presidency that was elected was at that point in time a tripartite presidency with an expansion of two?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was expanded, but it was set up of three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, three people. And those three people included Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the same time and on the same date, Ratko Mladic was appointed the general of the army, the head of the army; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander of the Main Staff, I think was the technical term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was that done by the Presidency, or was that done by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an Assembly decision, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that decision then ratified by the Presidency, or was the fact that the Assembly itself had made the determination that he would be the commander in chief of the army sufficient for him to take responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And he was, as I understand it from the information that you've given to us, he was subordinated to the Presidency. The Presidency was in a position to, and by law did, command him.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinate to the -- technically under the constitution, I think, to the president of the republic. The Presidency was exercising the powers of the president of the republic, pursuant to the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you so much. I appreciate that distinction because I think it is an important one. At some point in time, the Presidency became -- from three, became a single person, a single president; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that individual was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So from May 12th, 1992, up until December 17th of 1992, Mladic was responsible to the Presidency embodied in three individuals - Karadzic, Plavsic, and who was the third? Biljana Plavsic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then on December 17th, he was, at that point, subordinated to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not entirely correct. At the beginning of June the Presidency was expanded to five members --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that situation ended on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. That's when I was referring earlier to the tripartite Presidency, expanded by two. Thank you for that. What happened is Mladic was under the control of three, then five, and ultimately one; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the Republika Srpska Krajina, in 1992 who was the president, at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, Milan Babic was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during the time that he was president initially, who was the commander-in-chief of his army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been him. I'm not quite sure what the constitutional -- the state of the army per se was at that time. He remained president only until the middle of February --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after he left office, did there come about a shift in terms of a division between the Presidency and the military? And by that I mean was there an individual -- was the president, the individual, was the head of the military?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was similar to the situation that we've just been discussing in the RS. There was the president, and then there was a military commander who was also known, I believe, as the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the president after Milan Babic left was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the head of the Main Staff was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I can't recall offhand. There were several changes during the course of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But those individuals were then, if I'm understanding you correctly - and again, if I'm wrong, tell me I'm wrong - those individuals who were the head of the Main Staff were subordinate to the president under their constitution and their laws.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's who they were responsible to, and that's who directed them to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the constitution says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you repeat your last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The constitution says the president is the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the SFRY, the SFRY went through an evolution in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started an evolution way before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm really referring to here is Belgrade and the shift from the SFRY to FRY.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the constitution of the FRY was adopted on the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before the constitution was adopted, there were military troops that comprised the JNA throughout the region and specifically within the various republics we've just talked about; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to ask you to define that a little more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. In April 1992 were there JNA, for example, in BH?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.
